overview.text: Ultraviolet (UV) radiation is electromagnetic energy with wavelengths shorter than visible light but longer than X-rays. The World Health Organization defines its range as 100–400 nanometers; humans cannot see it. UV occurs naturally in sunlight and can also come from artificial sources. Scientists divide it into UVA, UVB, and UVC bands. As sunlight passes through the atmosphere, ozone and other gases absorb all UVC and most UVB, so the UV that reaches the ground is mainly UVA with some UVB. This makes the ozone layer an important shield, not a complete barrier. UV exposure can harm skin and eyes, and excessive exposure is associated with sunburn, skin cancers, cataracts, and immune-system effects.

key_facts.text: UV is invisible to humans and occupies the part of the electromagnetic spectrum between visible light and X-rays.
The bands are commonly defined as UVA (315–400 nm), UVB (280–315 nm), and UVC (100–280 nm).
Sunlight and artificial sources—including some lamps and tanning devices—produce UV radiation.
The atmosphere absorbs all UVC and most UVB from sunlight; UVA is less affected, so surface UV is mainly UVA with a smaller UVB component.
UVB can damage DNA; excessive UV exposure is associated with skin cancer and eye damage, including cataracts.
